forces.title: Shrinking European natural gas demand due to electrification
forces.description: European natural gas demand is projected to decline by an average of 2% annually until 2030, and continue this trend through 2040. This fundamental shift is driven by the acceleration of electrification across transport, buildings, data centers, and industry, which will reduce the need for gas. For gas utilities, this implies a long-term reduction in throughput volume and necessitates strategic adaptation towards other energy value chains.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: EU policies drive shift from natural gas in heating sector
forces.description: The European Commission's 2026 Heating and Cooling Strategy targets reducing reliance on fossil fuels, particularly natural gas, in the heating sector (currently 70% fossil-fuel reliant). This strategy promotes district heating, industrial waste heat recovery, geothermal, and other renewable heat sources. This policy-driven shift directly impacts the demand for natural gas delivered by utilities to residential and commercial customers, creating a significant headwind for volume growth.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Integrated utility models re-emerge, valuing regulated networks
forces.description: Market volatility and high capital intensity are driving a return to integrated utility models, where entities control generation, network operations, and retail. For gas utilities, this means predictable earnings from regulated transmission and distribution (T&D) assets are increasingly valued as they help offset the volatility of generation revenues. This trend strengthens the investment case for regulated network operators by improving balance sheet resilience and reducing the weighted average cost of capital.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Major utilities increase capital allocation to regulated gas networks
forces.description: Leading European utilities such as Enel and Iberdrola are increasingly prioritizing and allocating substantial capital to regulated transmission and distribution (T&D) assets, which include gas networks. This strategy is driven by the desire for more predictable earnings and stable, infrastructure-like returns, which help offset the volatility experienced in other parts of the energy value chain. This increased investment represents an upside for companies operating regulated gas infrastructure.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Geopolitical energy shocks pose indirect risk to Irish gas utilities
forces.description: Ireland's high import dependence on fossil fuels, particularly gas, exposes its energy sector to geopolitical shocks and price volatility. While state-backed gas transmission and distribution operators like GNI benefit from regulated revenue streams, protecting them from direct price fluctuations, prolonged high energy costs or supply risks could indirectly impact customer demand or lead to pressure for tariff adjustments, challenging the sector's long-term operating environment.

forces.title: Regulated revenue streams protect Irish gas utility from price volatility
forces.description: Gas Networks Ireland (GNI), a state-backed operator, benefits from regulated revenue streams, which provide insulation against the volatility of global oil and gas prices. This regulatory framework protects the utility's profitability by ensuring cost recovery and stable income, even amidst geopolitical energy shocks. This makes GNI comparatively well protected compared to other energy firms with direct commodity exposure, enhancing its financial resilience and investment appeal.

viewpoints.title: Declining gas demand necessitates diversification for European utilities
viewpoints.description: European utilities historically reliant on gas face a cautious outlook as natural gas demand is projected to shrink by 2% annually until 2030 and further decline through 2040. This forces traditional gas and power utilities to strategically expand into power value chain activities, shifting their focus away from solely gas-based operations. The need for this diversification is critical for long-term viability given the structural transformation in the energy landscape driven by electrification.
viewpoints.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

viewpoints.title: Irish gas utility GNI insulated by regulated revenue streams
viewpoints.description: Despite Ireland's high energy import dependence (approximately 80%) and continued reliance on fossil fuels, state-backed operators like Gas Networks Ireland (GNI) are relatively insulated. Their revenue streams are regulated, protecting them from the direct impact of oil and gas price volatility. While the broader energy sector faces challenges from geopolitical shocks and grid constraints, the regulated nature of GNI's business provides a degree of stability and predictability.

demand_drivers.description: The acceleration of electrification in transport, buildings, data centers, and industry is projected to increase electricity's share of final energy consumption, directly leading to a decline in natural gas demand.

demand_drivers.driver: Policy shifts towards renewables in heating
demand_drivers.description: European policy shifts, including a new Heating and Cooling Strategy for 2026, aim to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, particularly natural gas, in the heating sector by supporting integrated local heat planning and renewable heat sources.

market_sizing.methodology: European net electricity consumption and natural gas demand figures based on McKinsey’s Global Energy Perspective 2025. Natural gas demand converted from billion cubic meters to terawatt-hours. Figure is for EU-27 plus Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.
